read.sections.0.text.back: Objects made or used by people in the past are called artifacts. When you study an artifact, start with what you can see. An observation is a detail that you can notice yourself, with your eyes or your hands. The tin has a dent on its lid, the letters "ML" on its side and a hinge that has been repaired. All of these are observations. Next, you can make an inference, that is, an idea you build from clues. For example, you might say that the owner of this tin used it to carry lunch. That might be true, but the tin itself does not tell us.
read.sections.0.text.source: An object that people made or used in the past is called an artefact. When you study an artefact, start with what you can see. An observation is a detail that you can notice for yourself, with your eyes or your hands. The tin has a dent in the lid, the letters "ML" on its side and a repaired hinge. These are all observations. Next, you can make an inference, which is an idea that you build from clues. For example, you might say that the owner used this tin to carry lunch. That could be true, but the tin itself does not tell us.

read.sections.0.simpler.back: Old objects used by people are artifacts. First, look at the artifact. Say what you see. This is observation. The tin has a dent. There are the letters ML on it. Someone repaired its hinge. Next, you can guess the meaning of the clue. This is inference. Maybe its owner carried lunch in the tin. That might be true. But the tin does not tell us.

read.sections.1.text.back: A second source can help you test an inference. The notebook page states that Mina L. filled rice and beans in her tin before going to the repair workshop. The tin has the letters "ML", so maybe there is a connection between Mina and the tin. This connection should be checked, but it does not prove that the tin was hers. The letters might belong to someone else, and objects often move from one person to another person. Context can also help. Context is the information around an object, such as the place where the object was found. We know the tin and the notebook were found in the same box.
read.sections.1.text.source: A second source can help you test an inference. The notebook page says that Mina L. packed rice and beans in her tin before going to a repair workshop. The tin has the letters "ML", so there may be a link between Mina and the tin. This link is worth checking, but it does not prove that the tin was hers. The letters could belong to someone else, and objects often pass from one person to another. Context can help too. Context is the information around an object, such as where it was found. We know the tin and the notebook were found in the same box.

read.sections.1.simpler.back: Another source can help us check an idea. A notebook says Mina L. filled rice and beans in her tin. The tin has the letters ML. So, maybe the tin was hers. But we are not sure. ML might be someone else's name. People also give things to other people. Context also helps us. Context is what is around the object. The tin and the notebook were in the same box.
read.sections.1.simpler.source: Another source can help us check an idea. A notebook says Mina L. packed rice and beans in her tin. The tin has the letters ML. So maybe the tin was hers. But we cannot be sure. ML could stand for another person. People also give things to other people. Context helps us too. Context is what is around the object. The tin and notebook were in the same box.

read.sections.2.text.back: Careful historians are honest about uncertainty. The repair shows that someone chose to repair the tin and keep using it. However, it does not prove that its owner was poor or careless, because people repair things for many reasons. Museum labels often use careful words, such as "maybe" or "perhaps", when the evidence is not certain. A good label for the tin might read, "This tin may once have carried the lunch of someone who worked at a repair workshop." A dated record, or a list of the tin's previous owners, could strengthen this claim.
read.sections.2.text.source: A careful historian is honest about uncertainty. The repair shows that someone chose to fix the tin and keep using it. However, it does not prove that the owner was poor or careless, because people repair things for many reasons. Museum labels often use careful words, such as "may" or "probably", when the evidence is not certain. A good label for the tin might say, "This tin may have carried the lunch of someone who worked at a repair workshop." A dated record, or a list of the tin's past owners, could make this claim stronger.

read.sections.2.simpler.back: Be honest about uncertainty. Someone repaired the tin. So, someone wanted to keep it. That does not mean its owner was poor. People repair things for many reasons. Use careful words like maybe and perhaps. A label can read: This tin may once have carried someone's lunch. A record that has a date can help us know more.

watch.summary.back: This is the same short video as in Lesson 1. This video explains primary sources. A primary source is a thing made or used in the time period you are studying. An object can be a primary source, just like a letter or a diary. An object shows the material used to make it. The object also shows the marks and repairs on it. A piece of writing shows what its writer saw or did. In this lesson, the tin is one primary source and the notebook is another primary source. When you combine both of them, you can build an idea about who used the tin. But, finding two things in the same box does not prove that both belonged to the same person. So, careful historians state what can be seen, then make an inference, and then mention what is still not known.
watch.summary.source: This is the same short video as in Lesson 1. It explains primary sources. These are things made or used at the time you are studying. An object can be a primary source, just like a letter or a diary. An object shows what it is made of. It also shows its marks and repairs. A piece of writing shows what its writer saw or did. In this lesson, the tin is one primary source and the notebook is another. When you put them together, you can build an idea about who used the tin. But finding two things in the same box does not prove they had the same owner. So a careful historian says what can be seen, then makes an inference, and then names what is still unknown.
